subject: WSJ Travel: What’s an Airline Status Match? 🤔
body_text:
96 Plus, an airline lounge bonanza and (another) Disney price increase   Is this email difficult to read? View in browser             Sponsored by       Dawn Gilbertson   The Popular Tool United Is Using to Woo Delta Loyalists   Plus, an airline lounge bonanza and (another) Disney price increase   Happy Friday! Enjoy the long holiday weekend if you’re off. Hurricane Isaias and tropical storms on the West Coast might mess with travel plans, so monitor your flight status closely and check for cruise implications.  

   In travel news this week, a deeper picture emerged of the pilot accused of trying to take down a Tel Aviv-bound FlyDubai flight. First officer Hamam al-Hammami told investigators he almost carried out his attack in July but called it off because he cared about one member of the flight crew. As my colleague Andrew Tangel reports, rogue pilots are a growing safety threat . 

   American Airlines plans to install Starlink Wi-Fi service on all of its 1,000 mainline jets, up from the 500 it announced earlier this year. 

   Another week, another flood of airport-lounge additions. Good news for you Newark fliers: American Express now plans a 30,000-square-foot lounge, its largest, in Terminal A. The original plans called for an 18,000-square-foot lounge. (Those plans also called for it to open this year; the bigger lounge will debut in 2027.) Amex couldn’t resist a jab at the other credit-card companies nipping at its lounge heels: It will be the only operator with outlets at the three major metro New York airports. Amex also announced the addition of a second lounge at London’s Heathrow. 

   American is promising a lounge glow-up at its massive Charlotte, N.C., hub with plans for a new 40,000-square-foot Admirals Club. The lounge, which will be its largest, is due to open in 2028. 

   Lastly, Disney announced its annual theme-park price increases . 

       Status match basics     DAWN GILBERTSON/WSJ   You probably have heard about the kerfuffle between Delta and Elon Musk after the airline passed on Starlink service in favor of Amazon.

   United seized the moment to tout its Starlink service by going after Delta (and American) frequent fliers. It did so with something called a status match.

   Not familiar? Here’s how it works. If you have status on one airline, you can apply to instantly get the same level at a competing airline, temporarily at least. Airlines often run status-match promotions to get frequent fliers to switch sides or at least try the competition.

   Sometimes, they match your status plus one. American Airlines offered such a promotion through our corporate travel department in August. I have A List status on Southwest Airlines so applied by providing proof. Within a week or so, I was granted Platinum status on American through Dec. 16. (Gold is American’s base level.) The status has already given me free extra-legroom seats, checked bags, priority boarding and bonus miles. No upgrades yet.

   Here’s the catch: You have to rack up a certain number of loyalty points by the deadline to keep the status. You earn these by flying or spending money with one of the airline’s partners and by using one of its credit cards. (I signed up for one of American’s low-fee credit cards to help the cause and cash in on a welcome bonus.) 

   To keep platinum through March 2028, I need to rack up 25,000 loyalty points from the start of the challenge. I’ve earned 11,255, so need another 13,745.

   That might be out of reach even with two American flights coming up, including a flight in economy to Europe. But I’ve already reached the threshold for Gold (10,000 loyalty points), so that’s a small win. The promotion does have me using American more, a win for the airline. 

   You don’t have to have a corporate agency to be eligible for a status match. The latest United one targets Delta and American fliers, but there’s been a promotion running all year . So if you’re holding status in an airline and want to play the field, reach out to that airline’s frequent-flier program.

   Delta and American fliers have until Oct. 15 to match during United’s Starlink promotion. Once approved, you have to spend between $1,500 and $7,000 and fly within 90 days to keep the status.

   Do you play this game? Tell me your tips and tricks.

   This is an edition of the WSJ Travel newsletter, a weekly source of inspiration and advice for navigating your vacations and business trips, along with the latest travel news. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here . 

       Notes From the Road ✈️     DAWN GILBERTSON/WSJ   • Robotaxis may be coming to an airport near you. I took three rides to size up the pros and cons. 

   • American Airlines bumps way more passengers than most airlines. It says that dubious title is coming to an end .

   • A rabbi even mentioned it in his sermon: Behind the tension over Aspen’s runway overhaul .

   • You’ve done the beaches in Italy and France. Consider Turkey for your next upscale Mediterranean getaway .

   • Our writer went on a menopause wellness binge . Was it worth it?

       CONTENT FROM: SILVERSEA CRUISES     SILVERSEA BRINGS THE WORLD CLOSER   Explore over 900 destinations across all seven continents on board small ships that set the standard for elite ocean travel. From the Mediterranean and the Caribbean to Antarctica and the Galápagos, Silversea voyages are defined by immersive exploration, personalized service, all-inclusive indulgence, culinary innovation, and unmatched access to the world.   Discover More  >       One Good Tip 🎯   Hate stalking the airline seat map for a better seat ahead of your flight like it’s a part-time job? American Airlines will now automatically search for a seat in the same cabin if you opt into a new feature on its app after booking a flight and do so at least 24 hours before departure. It’s called automatic seat change . You pick aisle, middle or window and whether you only want to move to seats closer to the front. Don’t like bulkhead seats? Don’t check that box. Exit row seats are excluded. The airline says passengers are accommodated based on their frequent-flier status and when they signed up for the seat-change option. United Airlines unveiled a similar feature earlier this year.

       Travel Math 🧮   $500 million   Ticket sales for “The Wizard of Oz” at the Sphere in Las Vegas since its debut in August 2025. Some analysts are worried, though, that demand is cooling despite new features including 4D effects.

       And We Quote 💬   “I just don’t think the rest of the cabin needs to join your Teams meeting with you!”

   — Frequent flier Christopher Mosby, on the rise of in-flight video chats with co-workers and family thanks to speedy Wi-Fi.

       You Have Thoughts 🤔   …on online passport applications : 

   • “Just wanted to share that, despite being a bit skeptical, my husband and I renewed our U.S. passports online. We opted for standard delivery. Imagine our surprise when new passports showed up in our mailbox exactly one week after we applied! And updating the new numbers to all our frequent-flier accounts using their individual apps was seamless, too. Now my only question is: When I return to France next month, will the new EES system automatically recognize that I previously registered for that program this past summer using my old passport? Fingers crossed.” — Mindy Maloon, Georgia  

   …on maximizing those premium credit card benefits : 

   • “Thanks for your advice to check on unused benefits from your travel credit card. I was planning a one-week trip to France, and my Chase United Club Card had the same Intercontinental Hotel listed that I was planning to book, but with free breakfast, early check-in, and late checkout and elite status. I usually book the night before my arrival at European hotels so I can get right into my room early after the overnight flight. Your advice saved me one night’s charge.” — Michael Hyman, North Carolina 

   …on Waymo’s wayward routes : 

   • “Nice column today about how Waymo took you through local streets. Sometimes, actual drivers do that as well. In November 1990, I had a meeting in Paris that ended at 9:30 a.m., and I had to get to CDG to catch the 11:40 a.m. Concorde to JFK. (Don’t get the impression that I routinely flew the rocket. I managed to score that ticket only four times.) Unfortunately, the president of France was also on his way to the airport that morning to fly out on his Concorde, so all the main roads were closed to traffic. My taxi driver was amazing, however; she zigged and zagged through tiny local streets and byways and got me there in time.” —Robert Kantowitz, New York 

   (Responses have been condensed and edited.) 

       Cheers and Jeers 🤷   Cheers to Southwest Airlines for a new-to-me feature. In the help center on its app, there’s a “We’ll call you” feature under “Need more assistance?” You just type in your name and phone number and you get a call back. (This is different from calling a company and being offered the option for a call back during long waits.) A Southwest rep called me back almost instantly and was able to quickly clear up a seat-assignment issue for an upcoming flight.

   Big jeers to hotels where front-desk clerks greet you not with a warm hello, but a rote, “ID and credit card, please.” No different than those doctors’ offices that ask you for your ID and insurance card as soon you approach the counter. In my experience, it happens too often regardless of a hotel’s daily rate and sets the wrong mood for the stay.
